summary: A first-person travelogue of visits to five reputedly haunted landmarks in late 2023: the Tower of London, Versailles, the Stanley Hotel, Waverly Hills Sanatorium and Savannah's Mercer-Williams House. The author begins as a skeptic hoping to be proven wrong, hears local ghost legends from guides, and has a few ambiguous experiences. By the end they feel unsettled by the limits of their former skepticism.
one_line: A skeptic's 2023 tour of haunted landmarks, from the Tower of London to Savannah, ends with shaken certainty about the supernatural.
key_facts: On October 3, 2023 the author joined a night guided tour at The Tower of London led by a theatrical guide named Reginald.
Reginald told of Anne Boleyn, the headless queen said to walk the tower's halls, and the White Lady, who waves to children from the turrets.
A soldier named Humphrey reportedly encountered what he insisted was Anne Boleyn's ghost in November 1817 and was found by comrades in a state of shock.
At the Palace of Versailles, two female academics claimed in 1901 to have stumbled into an apparent time-slip to the days of Marie Antoinette.
Groundskeeper Martine told the author of a ghostly coach and galloping hooves heard on moonlit nights, and said she had heard the galloping multiple times since starting work at Versailles.
The Stanley Hotel in the Rocky Mountains inspired Stephen King's "The Shining"; Room 217 is where King spent a restless night, and ghostly self-playing pianos are reported.
At the Stanley Hotel the author heard piano music from the ballroom late at night, but found the ballroom empty and the music stopped.
Waverly Hills Sanatorium in Kentucky was a tuberculosis hospital; guide Eleanor's grandmother was a nurse there in the 1930s.
Room 502 at Waverly Hills is tied to a tale of a nurse who succumbed to despair; visitors claim to see her figure in the doorway and hear wails.
At Room 502 on November 8, 2023, a gust of wind was followed by a sound like a sob, which the author could not explain.

On December 13, 2023 in Savannah, Georgia, the author took a walking tour led by Josephine, who claimed heightened sensitivity to spirits, centered on the Mercer-Williams House and Jim Williams's purportedly haunted antique collection.
By the end the author was unsettled not by fear of the supernatural but by the limits of their previous staunch skepticism.
